newsitem.title: TAJIKISTAN: Tajik govt troops seen in rebel colonel's town.
newsitem.headline: Tajik govt troops seen in rebel colonel's town.

text.p: Government armour on Friday entered the southern Tajikistan town of Kurgan Tyube, stronghold of rebel Colonel Makhmud Khudoyberdyev, residents said.
Contacted by telephone, they said Khudoyberdyev, his family and guards had fled his house in the town and moved into the barracks of his elite brigade on its outskirts.
Armed looters went through Khodoyberdyev's house after he vacated it. The residents heard no fighting but said they had seen at least three government tanks near the town's only bus station.
The politically ambitious Khudoyberdyev moved his armour towards Dushanbe, 110 km (70 miles) to the north, last weekend after fighting between two rival warlords in the capital.
But he appeared to suffer some military defeats in four days of fighting and President Imomali Rakhmonov issued a decree dismissing the colonel on Wednesday.

On Thursday, Khodoyberdyev refused to obey the order and said he was ready to resume fighting because the government had failed to withdraw its troops from around Kurgan Tyube, as agreed on Wednesday.
The defiant commander warned of fresh fighting if government troops failed to withdraw to Dushanbe. "Honestly, I think it could only be war," the colonel said in an interview in Kurgan Tyube.
His armed supporters vowed earlier on Friday troops not to give up their weapons as long as government forces failed to honour their side of Wednesday's agreement.

Russia's Interfax news agency quoted the rebel brigade's chief of staff, Ergash Khasanov, as saying "our corps will not hand over its weapons" because heavy artillery and pro-government forces have not been withdrawn.

Itar-Tass news agency said negotiations between Khudoyberdyev and a senior commander from Russian-led peacekeeping forces had failed. The talks near Khudoyberdyev's headquarters in Kurgan Tyube lasted just five minutes, it said.
Moscow has played a low-key role but is concerned about stability in Tajikistan, which borders Afghanistan and is seen by Russia as a buffer against spreading Islamic fundamentalism.
Khudoberdyev told Interfax on Friday that there was some shooting in the southern region but put the incidents down to "illegal armed bands which are robbing the local population".
Khudoyberdyev's house in Kurgan Tyube came under attack on Thursday from what the rebel leader said were government troops.
Fighting erupted in Dushanbe only weeks after Rakhmonov signed a peace agreement with Islamic opposition guerrillas aimed at ending four years of civil war in Tajikistan.

The guerrillas were not involved in the latest clashes, but Khudoyberdyev joined the fray, moving his brigade towards the capital last Saturday. The motive for his latest mutiny -- his third in two years -- remained unclear.

On Friday Rakhmonov sacked Khudoberdyev ally Yakub Salimov, who led the loosing group of the two which had clashed in Dushanbe. A Rakhmonov official said Environment Minister Ismoil Davlatov had been appointed to replace Salimov.

Rakhmonov blamed the unrest on a "third force" opposed to his peace deal with the Islamists and mafia groups operating in the republic, which is spread across the Tien Shan and Pamir mountain ranges bordering China and Afghanistan.
"Active agitation, led by a 'third force' against the Tajik peace accord, has helped to bring about this mood of revenge," Rakhmonov told Friday's Russian daily Izvestia.
Khudoyberdyev opposes the return of armed Islamist guerrillas to Dushanbe, agreed under the peace deal.
He used the issue to declare autonomy for his southwestern region around Kurgan Tyube last month, setting up a "Defence Council" to run it in a move deemed "unconstitutional" by Dushanbe.
Western observers say also that rival warlords -- all nominally loyal to Rakhmonov -- are battling for turf in the republic, its economy shattered by the civil war.
